passage: Kamal's head dropped onto his arm twice during the chemistry lesson. His test slip had come back that morning, 38 out of 100, and he had folded it into his geometry box. Under the desk his phone lit up again: Reena, 2:14 a.m. the night before, then 3:40. He had answered every message, telling her things would be okay, and telling his mother he was studying late. Nobody knew how bad Reena's nights were, not even her parents; she had made him promise. Mr Thomas kept him back after the bell. "You're not yourself, Kamal." "I'm fine, sir, just tired." Mr Thomas said the counsellor's room was open to him, and to any friend he was worried about, and Kamal nodded at the floor. In his pocket the phone buzzed again.

passage:
Dear Rukmini,
I need to tell you something before you hear it from anyone else, and I need you to read to the end.
For three months I've been the person you message at one in the morning, and two, and three. I wanted to be. I thought if I answered every time, you'd be okay, and nobody else had to know how bad it's been. I didn't tell anyone, not once.
But I'm falling apart. I barely sleep. I failed two unit tests. And you're not better; you're still where you were in June, and you still haven't talked to anyone who actually knows how to help. That's partly on me, because I let myself be enough when I'm not.
So tonight I told my mother everything. She called your mother straight away, and they are talking now, while I write this. Tomorrow the counsellor will see you.
I'm still your friend. I'm just not your only one any more.
Jatin

qa.q: How long has Jatin been answering Rukmini's late-night messages?
How is Jatin feeling as he writes the letter?
qa.a: Jatin is exhausted and guilty, falling apart from lack of sleep and feeling responsible that Rukmini hasn't got real help.

qa.q: What should Jatin have done back in June?
qa.a: Told a parent or the counsellor early, so Rukmini got professional help while Jatin stayed a friend rather than the only support.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Rukmini may feel hurt or betrayed at first, but also cared for, and less alone once adults are involved.

grounding: Shows a student becoming a friend's only support through the night and hiding it, until his sleep and marks collapse while the friend still has no professional help.

Tanvir, you asked why I look so wrecked lately. I'm Chaitanya, and I'll tell you, because I think I have to tell someone.
Since Diwali I've been Nakul's person. Whenever things get dark for him, and that's most nights, he messages me, and I answer. Midnight, two, four. I thought if I just stayed on, he'd be okay. I didn't tell anyone, because he asked me not to, and because I thought I could handle it.
I can't. I fall asleep in first period. My physics mark dropped to a thirty-one. I'm snapping at my sister. And Nakul still hasn't spoken to a single doctor or counsellor. Months of me, and nothing's actually better.
So last night I finally told my mum. She called Nakul's mother while I sat there, and this morning she emailed Mr Sen. He's expecting me at lunch. Will you walk there with me? I don't want to go in alone.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya's physics mark drop to?
How is Chaitanya feeling after months of late-night messages?
qa.a: Chaitanya is exhausted and overwhelmed, snapping at family and realising the effort hasn't helped Nakul.

qa.q: What would have been a better approach from the start?
qa.a: Telling a parent or teacher early, so Nakul got professional help while Chaitanya stayed a friend instead of the only lifeline.

qa.q: What might it mean for Tanvir to hear this?
qa.a: Tanvir learns why Chaitanya looked wrecked and can offer company on the walk to Mr Sen, a small but real support.

grounding: Shows a student becoming a friend's only support through the night and hiding it, until his sleep and marks slide and the friend still has no professional help.
